overview: Thecodontosaurus ('socket-toothed lizard') was a small sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Late Triassic of what is now England, living approximately 227–205 million years ago. It reached about 2.5 metres in length and was lightly built, moving primarily on its hind legs. The type species, Thecodontosaurus antiquus, was among the very first dinosaur genera ever named, described from fissure-fill deposits near Bristol, United Kingdom.

Thecodontosaurus is scientifically significant as one of the earliest named dinosaurs (1843) and as a basal sauropodomorph whose anatomy sheds light on the origins of the giant herbivorous lineage that would later include titanosaurs. Its discovery in the Bristol fissure fills — ancient cave infills of Late Triassic age — has provided important context for understanding Triassic palaeoenvironments in what is now Britain.

fossilSites.note: Additional Late Triassic fissure fills in Wales have produced material referred to Thecodontosaurus.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Thecodontosaurus was described in 1843 by Samuel Stutchbury and Henry Riley from fragmentary specimens collected in limestone fissure fills near Clifton, Bristol. It was named for its distinctive teeth set in deep sockets — a feature then considered unusual. The original holotype material was destroyed in the Bristol Museum during World War II bombing raids in 1940, though casts and referrals from other specimens allow continued study.

articles.title: Anatomy and Diet
articles.body: Thecodontosaurus was a relatively small, lightly built dinosaur with a long neck, slender limbs, and leaf-shaped, serrated teeth suited to herbivory or possibly omnivory. Its bipedal stance and proportions place it among the most basal sauropodomorphs. Study of juvenile specimens from the Pantydraco locality has illuminated growth patterns in early sauropodomorphs.

articles.title: Palaeoenvironment
articles.body: The fissure-fill deposits of the Bristol region represent ancient cave systems and crevices in Carboniferous limestone that accumulated terrestrial sediments during the Late Triassic. These deposits also contain remains of other small vertebrates, and the fauna suggests a warm, semi-arid island environment in what was then a tropical archipelago in the Tethys Sea region.

articles.title: Scientific Significance
articles.body: As one of the earliest-named dinosaurs, Thecodontosaurus played a role in shaping early understanding of the group. Modern phylogenetic analyses place it as a very early-diverging sauropodomorph, more primitive than Plateosaurus, which makes it informative for reconstructing the ancestral body plan of the entire sauropod lineage.

record.description: Thecodontosaurus antiquus was a small basal sauropodomorph from Rhaetian fissure deposits near Bristol, represented by abundant disarticulated bones and newly described partial skeletons.
facts: Many original Bristol fossils were destroyed in 1940, but surviving and newer material documents much of the anatomy.
A categorical omnivore label is not established; tooth form permits plant-dominated or mixed feeding interpretations.

review.ageReviewNote: The type assemblage is Rhaetian, much narrower and younger than 227-205 Ma.
